notes.meaning: Jesus tells his followers a parable about a rich landowner and his estate manager. Someone reported that this manager was wasting his master's property. Jesus wants his listeners to think about how they handle the things God places in their care.

The master calls the manager in to demand his financial records and fires him. The manager must give a full report before he is sent away. This reminds us that everyone must one day give an account to God for how they used their life and gifts.

The manager wonders what he will do once he loses his job. He feels too weak to do hard farm labor and too proud to beg in the street. Rather than repenting of his dishonesty, he looks for an easy way out of his trouble.

The manager suddenly comes up with a clever plan. He wants to make sure people in the area will welcome him into their homes when he is out of work. He resolves to use his remaining time in office to win their favor.
The manager sends for each person who owes his master goods. He asks the first debtor how much he owes. These debts were likely payments of rent from the harvest of the land.

The first debtor owes a large amount of olive oil, and the manager tells him to cut the bill in half. By changing the written contract quickly, the debtor gets a massive discount. This makes the man deeply grateful to the manager while cheating the owner out of his share.

He then turns to another debtor who owes a huge supply of wheat and tells him to lower his bill by twenty percent. Changing the contracts gives each tenant a heavy saving. In this way, the manager builds a group of people who are in his debt and will owe him kindness later.

The master finds out what happened and praises the dishonest manager for acting shrewdly. He does not praise the man's stealing, but his foresight in planning ahead for his future. Jesus observes that worldly people often show more energy and practical sense in earthly matters than believers show in pursuing God's kingdom.

Jesus tells his disciples to use earthly money to do good and help others while they can. Earthly wealth is temporary and will soon be gone, but using it generously brings lasting spiritual reward. When life on earth ends, those who have been helped and blessed will welcome faithful stewards into their eternal home.

A person who proves honest and reliable in small everyday matters will also be reliable in big responsibilities. On the other hand, someone who cheats in little things will cheat when trusted with much more. Our daily integrity in small duties reveals what kind of character we truly have.

Jesus applies this rule directly to money and spiritual life. If a person cannot be trusted to handle worldly wealth faithfully, God will not trust them with true spiritual riches. Real riches are the lasting spiritual blessings of God's grace and truth.

Jesus points out that earthly goods do not really belong to us; they belong to God, who places them in our temporary care. If people fail to manage what belongs to another, they will not be given an eternal inheritance of their own. God looks for faithful caretakers before granting eternal rewards.

A household servant cannot have two bosses with competing interests. If he tries, he will end up loving one and hating the other, or staying loyal to one while ignoring the other. In the same way, a person cannot be devoted to God while serving the love of money.

The Pharisees heard Jesus speaking about money and mocked him with sneering faces. They loved wealth and assumed that being rich was a clear sign of God's favor. Jesus' warnings about the spiritual dangers of wealth directly challenged their lifestyle and pride.

Jesus tells the Pharisees that they work hard to look righteous in the eyes of people, but God sees what is hidden in their hearts. Human praise often celebrates things like outward status and wealth. Yet in God's eyes, hypocritical pride and greed are completely detestable.

The era of the Law of Moses and the prophets pointed forward until the coming of John the Baptist. With John, the good news of God's kingdom began to be openly announced, and eager crowds were pressing hard to enter it. The arrival of the gospel called for an urgent, wholehearted response.

Even though a new era has arrived, God's moral law has not lost any of its authority. Heaven and earth could vanish more easily than the smallest stroke of God's word could fail. Jesus came to fulfill and uphold the true intent of God's law, not to cancel it.

Jesus gives an example of the law's standard by addressing divorce. A man who divorces his wife and marries someone else commits adultery, and marrying a divorced woman is also adultery. Jesus refuses to allow casual dismissals of marriage vows, defending the sacred bond God created.

differ.view: Remarriage after divorce is considered adultery in all circumstances, as marriage is an unconditional covenant that lasts until death.
Divorce and remarriage are allowed when a spouse has committed marital unfaithfulness or has deserted the marriage.

notes.meaning: Jesus tells of a wealthy man who dressed in royal purple and expensive linen, enjoying great luxury every single day. His life was centered entirely on personal comfort and outward splendor. He lived for his own pleasures without any thought for God or needy neighbors.

Outside the rich man's gate lay a destitute, sick man named Lazarus whose body was covered in open sores. He desperately hoped to eat scraps from the rich man's feast, while street dogs gathered to lick his wounds. The contrast showed the rich man's complete lack of mercy toward someone suffering right outside his door.

Lazarus eventually dies, and angels carry him to the place of honor right beside Abraham at the heavenly banquet. The rich man dies as well and receives an elaborate earthly funeral. In an instant, the earthly conditions of both men are completely reversed.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Abraham's side, or Abraham's bosom, is understood as the limbo of the fathers, where the righteous dead waited until Christ redeemed them and opened heaven.

notes.meaning: In the realm of the dead, the rich man finds himself in severe torment and misery. Looking up from a distance, he sees Abraham far away with Lazarus resting at his side. He is forced to witness the eternal joy of the very beggar he once ignored.

The rich man cries out to Abraham as his forefather, begging for pity and asking that Lazarus dip his fingertip in water to cool his tongue. The agony in the flame is intense, yet he asks only for a tiny drop of relief. He still treats Lazarus like an errand runner rather than an equal.

Abraham answers gently but firmly, reminding the man that he had enjoyed all his good things during his earthly life while Lazarus suffered through terrible hardships. The rich man had chosen earthly comfort as his highest good and neglected God. Now justice has arrived, bringing comfort to Lazarus and torment to the rich man.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older critical scholars saw the passage as simply describing a mechanical reversal of fortunes between rich and poor, rather than a moral and spiritual judgment.

notes.meaning: Abraham adds that a massive, unbridgeable chasm has been firmly fixed between them. No one can cross over from the place of comfort to the place of torment, and no one can escape from agony into blessedness. A person's spiritual destiny is final and permanent once this life ends.

Realizing his own condition cannot be changed, the rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus back to the living world. He asks that Lazarus visit his father's household to deliver an urgent message. He hopes a messenger from the unseen world might succeed where other warnings failed.

He explains that he has five brothers who are still living in the same careless and selfish way. He wants Lazarus to warn them directly about what lies ahead so they will not end up in the same place of torment. He knows that without a change of heart, their fate will be just as tragic as his.

Abraham answers that his brothers already have the books of Moses and the prophets. The Scriptures contain God's clear revelation of how to live, repent, and love one's neighbor. If his brothers want to escape judgment, they need to listen to and obey God's written word.

The rich man objects and argues that reading Scripture will not be enough to break through their stubbornness. He insists that if someone actually returns from the dead to warn them, they will truly repent. He assumes a dramatic, supernatural sign will succeed where God's ordinary message failed.

Abraham concludes that if people refuse to hear Moses and the prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead. Hardened hearts reject God's truth because of unbelief, not from a lack of evidence. A miraculous sign cannot create true faith in someone who obstinately closes their heart to God's word.
